pageHelp.activity: This page shows what indexarr has done: feed updates, searches received from apps, grabs and logs. Use the tabs to find a failed run or a slow search, and read the cause and the suggested action. It exists so problems can be diagnosed without reading the server logs.
pageHelp.app: This page connects indexarr to Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr and the other apps, and lists the download clients. Use Connect an app to let indexarr create and update the indexers inside the app; use the manual address only for apps that accept a Torznab URL. It exists so you do not copy addresses and keys by hand.
pageHelp.app_form: This page connects one app to indexarr. Enter the address you use in the browser and the app API key; indexarr creates the indexers inside it and keeps them updated. Use it once per app, and open the connection again only when its address or key changes.
pageHelp.client_form: This page adds a download client, the program that receives the torrent or NZB. Choose the software, enter its address and password or key, and say which protocol it handles. Use it when downloads should start automatically instead of being saved by hand.
pageHelp.definition: This page shows one site definition: its state, version, categories and settings. Use Create indexer to start from it, or the advanced tools to inspect it. It exists for diagnosing a site that does not behave as expected.
pageHelp.definition_form: This page creates or replaces a definition from its YAML. Paste the definition, validate it, and save it only if you trust its source. Use it when a site is not in the catalogue yet.
pageHelp.definitions: This page lists the site definitions that indexarr can use. Use it to check the state and version of a definition, or to create an indexer from one. It is a tool for advanced users: normal use starts from Add indexer.
pageHelp.discover: This page shows the feeds found on a site address. Choose the feed you want and add it as an indexer. Use it when a site has no native definition but publishes an RSS or Atom feed.
pageHelp.home: This page tells you at a glance whether indexarr is working and what to do next. Read the status box first, then the suggested next step; use the address and key here when an app asks for them. It exists so you do not have to read logs or documentation to know where you stand.
pageHelp.import: This page imports indexers from Prowlarr or Jackett without changing them. Choose the manager, review the preview, then apply the plan. Use it when you already have a working manager and do not want to add every site again.
pageHelp.indexer_add: This page helps you choose a site without reading a catalogue of two hundred names. Start from what you need, read the one-line reason and what the site requires, try five real results, then add it; Show all sites opens the full catalogue. Use the guided path the first time and the full list when you already know the site you want.
pageHelp.indexer_detail: This page is the working page of one site: its health, the latest releases, the filters and its settings. Use Test and the refresh action to check it, and Edit to change its credentials or categories. It exists so every problem and every setting of a site stays in one place.
pageHelp.indexer_form: This page adds or edits one site. Fill only the fields the site requires, leave the rest in Advanced, and press Add and test to save and check it immediately. Use it when a site needs an account, a cookie or a special address. The frequency decides how often this source refreshes on its own: it applies to this source only and does not slow the live app searches.
pageHelp.indexers: This page lists the sites indexarr can search, one row per site, with their health. logs.problem.timeout: The site took too long to answer.
logs.advice.timeout: Usually temporary. If it keeps happening, the site is slow or overloaded: raise its timeout in the source settings or check your proxy.
logs.problem.canceled: The operation was interrupted before it finished.
logs.advice.canceled: This happens when the app closes its request early or indexarr is stopping. Nothing to do unless it happens all the time.
logs.problem.refused: The service refused the connection: it is off or the port is wrong.
logs.advice.refused: Check that the service (site, proxy, FlareSolverr or download client) is running and that address and port are right.
logs.problem.dns: The site name cannot be resolved: the domain changed or DNS is not reachable.
logs.advice.dns: Check whether the site moved to a new domain and update the source address, or check the network and DNS of this machine.
logs.problem.tls: The secure connection failed: the site certificate is invalid or expired.
logs.advice.tls: Often the site itself has a problem and fixes it soon. If the site uses a self-signed certificate, check the address (http/https).
logs.problem.blocked: The site is blocking automatic access (anti-bot protection such as Cloudflare).
logs.advice.blocked: Configure FlareSolverr in Settings › Network and enable it for this source, or use a proxy.
logs.problem.auth: Login refused: username, password or cookie are no longer valid.
logs.advice.auth: Open the source, check the credentials (or paste a fresh cookie) and run the test.
logs.problem.rate: The site is limiting the number of requests (too many in a short time).
logs.advice.rate: Lower the update frequency or the daily query limit of this source; the limit usually resets by itself.
logs.problem.server: The site is having a problem of its own (server error).
logs.advice.server: Nothing to change in indexarr: wait for the site to recover. If it lasts for days, the site may be closed.
logs.problem.notfound: The requested page does not exist (any more).
logs.advice.notfound: The site may have changed its structure or removed the release: check the source address and, if it repeats, update the definition.
logs.advice.reset: Usually temporary (unstable network or overloaded site). If it repeats, check the proxy or VPN.
logs.problem.parse: The page was received, but its content was not what the definition expects.
logs.advice.parse: The site probably changed its layout. Run the source test; if it fails, the definition needs an update.
logs.problem.dbbusy: The database was busy with another operation.
logs.advice.dbbusy: indexarr retries by itself. If it happens often, avoid opening the database with other programs while indexarr runs.
logs.advice.database: Run the integrity check in Maintenance. If the error persists, restore a recent backup.
logs.problem.vault: An encrypted secret could not be opened.
logs.advice.vault: Check that the vault key is the one used when the passwords were saved; otherwise enter the passwords again.
logs.problem.queue: Too many operations at the same time: this one was skipped.
logs.advice.queue: Normal during bursts of requests. If it happens all the time, raise the live search limit in Settings.
logs.problem.flood: The site accepts one search every so often (flood control): this one was queued or refused by the site.
logs.advice.flood: Normal with DDUnlimited, which takes about one search a minute. Queued searches run by themselves in the background and the next request reads them from the cache. Nothing to do, unless the site refuses every time.
logs.problem.disk: The disk is full or the folder cannot be written.
logs.advice.disk: Free some space or fix the permissions of the data folder.
logs.problem.unknown: Something went wrong; the original error message is shown below.
logs.advice.unknown: If it happens only once, you can ignore it. If it repeats, download the log and include it when you report the problem.
logs.advice.repeat: Nothing to do if it happens once; if it repeats, check the area shown on the left.
logs.attr.title: Title
logs.attr.name: Name
logs.detailsHelp: The original log line and its fields, as written to the journal: useful when you report a problem.
logs.areaHelp: Which part of indexarr wrote this line.
logs.levelHelpRow: Info: normal activity. Warning: something did not work but indexarr carries on. Error: an operation failed and needs attention. Debug: extra detail for diagnosis.
logs.readText: Each line says in plain words what indexarr did. When something goes wrong, the line explains the problem and what you can do; the original technical text is kept under “Technical details” and in the downloaded file.
logs.live.reason.late: indexarr answered the app without waiting for this source (it is usually slower). The source kept searching in the background and its results are saved for the next request. Not an error.
logs.live.reason.queued: Many searches were running at the same time, so this source started after the app had its answer. It runs as soon as a slot is free. Not an error.
logs.live.reason.feedOnly: Feed-only source: it does not search live, its results come from the catalogue filled by the automatic updates.
logs.live.reason.paused: Paused for a while after repeated errors, to avoid hammering the site; it is retried automatically.
logs.live.reason.queue: Too many live searches at once: skipped for this request only.
logs.live.reason.abandoned: The app had already received its answer, so this search was not started.
logs.req.totalHelp: Results returned to the app, after merging duplicates.
logs.req.sourcesHelp: How the sources asked live behaved: green answered in time, grey kept working in the background or were skipped by design, red had a real error.
logs.req.openHelp: Click to see every source of this request.
logs.req.inTimeHelp: Sources that answered before the response was sent to the app.
logs.req.skippedHelp: Sources that do not search live by design (feed-only, paused after errors, too many searches at once). Not an error.
logs.req.failedHelp: Sources that really failed (login refused, site blocked, site down…). Open the row to see why.
logs.req.cacheOnlyHelp: No live search for this request: the answer came from the catalogue (for example an RSS poll or a request without text).
logs.req.stateHelp: In time, in background, queued, skipped or error: only “error” is a real problem.
logs.req.modeHelp: How the source was asked; “fallback” means a simpler search was used because the source does not support the requested one.
logs.req.sentHelp: The search text actually sent to this source (it can differ from the app's text, for example with the episode number).
logs.req.resultsHelp: Results each source contributed to the answer.
logs.stats.downloadsHelp: Torrents, magnets and NZBs of this source that your apps actually downloaded through indexarr in the window.
logs.stats.columnsHelp: Only the red “Failures” column is a problem. “In background” means indexarr answered the app without waiting for a slower source, which kept searching and saved its results for the next request; “Skipped” means the source does not search live by design. “Downloads” is the number that tells you whether a source is worth keeping.
logs.tab.downloadsHelp: What your apps actually downloaded through indexarr, and from which source.
logs.guideStep4: which sources your apps actually downloaded from: the best clue for deciding which sources to keep.
logs.dl.subtitle: Every torrent, magnet, NZB or eD2k link your apps took through indexarr, newest first, with the source that provided it.
logs.dl.windowHelp: The counters and the source table follow this window.
logs.dl.totalHelp: Torrents, magnets, NZBs and eD2k links delivered in the window; the download from the list and the send to aMule count too.
logs.dl.torrentsHelp: A .torrent file sent by indexarr to the app.
logs.dl.magnetsHelp: A magnet link handed to the app through indexarr's download link.
logs.dl.ed2kHelp: An eD2k link delivered to aMule: from the release list, with “Send to aMule”, or by an app that asks indexarr's download link before queueing it. A client that opens the ed2k attribute directly stays invisible.
logs.dl.nzbHelp: NZB files served to Usenet apps.
logs.dl.sourcesHelp: How many different sources provided at least one download.
logs.dl.directText: The feed also gives each result its magnet link, and many apps (gextto included) use it directly without passing through indexarr: those downloads cannot appear here. To count them, enable “Send magnet downloads through indexarr”.
logs.dl.bySourceHelp: A source that is queried often but never downloaded from is probably not worth keeping; one that provides many downloads is precious even if it is slow.
logs.dl.shareHelp: This source's share of all downloads in the window.
logs.dl.empty: No download went through indexarr in this window.
logs.dl.viaHelp: How indexarr handed the download to the app.
logs.dl.aboutText: A download is recorded when an app asks indexarr's download link of a result (indexarr sends the .torrent or NZB file, or redirects to the magnet or the eD2k link) and when you download an eD2k release from the list or send it to aMule. It means that release was chosen and handed to a download client; whether the client then completes it is up to the client.
logs.dl.ed2kDirect: The feed also carries the direct ed2k:// link in the ed2k attribute, and a client that uses it queues the file without telling indexarr. Gextto asks the download link first, so its grabs are counted; other clients need to do the same.
logs.dl.aboutDecide: Compare this table with the source statistics: queries, real errors and downloads together tell you which sources earn their place.
settings.proxyMagnetsTip: Off by default, because some apps use the magnet in the feed to recognise duplicates before downloading.
settings.proxyMagnetsHelp: When on, the feed no longer carries the magnet link directly: the app downloads through indexarr's link, which redirects to the magnet and records the download, so Logs › Downloads shows which source fed it. The infohash stays in the feed. Sonarr, Radarr and gextto follow the redirect.
settings.proxyEd2kTip: On by default: the eD2k link stays in the ed2k attribute, so gextto and other eD2k clients keep working.
settings.proxyEd2kHelp: When on, the feed link is indexarr's download link, which redirects to the ed2k:// link and records the grab, so Logs › Downloads shows which source fed it. The direct link remains in the ed2k attribute. Turn it off if a client cannot follow the redirect.

maintenance.help.resetStats: Use it when the numbers are skewed, for example after an app sent far more requests than usual. It clears the app requests, the per-source searches and the downloads; scheduled runs, health history, sources and releases stay.
